personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Before any measurement programme can function, every instrument must have an established baseline from controlled initial conditions. Pendulum_lab is the most straightforward instrument to characterize first—period is stable, well-understood physics, and insensitive to most environmental drift over a single session. Twelve trials will give adequate statistical grounding for future comparisons. Cannot proceed with any replication-based claims until baselines exist for all four instruments; starting with the simplest ensures I establish the measurement discipline and calibration protocol that will govern the others.

pendulum_lab has only 14 baseline trials from day 1. To establish a robust baseline and begin detecting drift, I need substantially more data—at least 24–30 trials total across days 1–10. The observatory instruments (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) have only 2 trials each and are severely under-sampled; the lab resonator has only 2 trials. pendulum_lab is my best-characterized instrument and the most informative to expand. Running 10 more trials today will move me toward the minimum sample size needed for reliable drift detection and cross-instrument comparison, which is essential before I can publish or trust any derived claims.

pendulum_lab has 26 baseline readings with stable mean 1.6724 beats and good resolution (0.000020 spacing). I need to continue accumulating post-baseline data on the same instrument to establish drift behaviour and maintain continuity of the precision programme. Six trials keeps measurement load manageable on day 3 while building the n needed for drift detection. No anomalies yet warrant hypothesis revision; continuing systematic measurement is the methodical priority.

resonator_lab has only 6 baseline trials so far (days 1–10 window allows ~10 total). Need to reach adequate baseline N before post-baseline phase. pendulum_lab is already at 34 trials and approaching saturation for baseline period. resonator_lab is the rate-limiting instrument for establishing robust baselines across the instrument suite. Six more trials will bring it to 12 total, sufficient to assess within-instrument stability and detect any drift or systematic offset that might affect cross-checks later.

Day 5 of 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 36 trials already (sufficient for baseline), but I need continuous daily coverage through day 10 to establish proper drift characterization and maintain the ledger tradition. The cross-check correlations are all within noise (all near ±0.3–0.4, within ±0.707 chance), suggesting no systematic relationships yet—this is expected at n=8 per pair. Running 6 more trials maintains measurement cadence, keeps the instrument warm in the cycle, and builds toward the full baseline specification. No anomalies detected; this is routine baseline work.

pendulum_lab has 44 trials and is approaching the end of the baseline period (days 1–10). I need to complete a full baseline before day 11 to establish drift rates and post-baseline comparisons. The instrument shows tight clustering (mean 1.6685, spacing 0.000020) with no level change, suggesting stable operation. Six more trials will bring me to 50 total, providing robust baseline statistics. This is methodologically essential: no instrument without a complete baseline is reliable once we enter post-baseline observation.

Baseline collection (days 1–10). resonator_obs has only 12 trials recorded; adding 8 more brings it to 20, providing robust baseline statistics before the window closes on Day 10. Observatory instruments can be batch-sampled efficiently.

resonator_obs shows the highest within-day variance (range 3.9876–4.1212 on day 7, SD ~0.048) and I need to establish robust baseline statistics before day 10 closes. Currently at 22 trials; 6 more will bring me to 28 trials, giving me stronger constraint on the true mean and allowing detection of any genuine drift. The large spread (4.0248 to 4.1212) relative to spacing (0.000048) suggests real physical variation or environmental sensitivity I should characterize during baseline, not after. This is methodologically prior to any hypothesis-building.

resonator_obs is at n=30 trials for baseline establishment (days 1–10). Today is day 9, so I have limited time to complete the baseline protocol before the cutoff. The ledger readings from day 8 show the instrument is stable (4.1171, 4.1244 cycles/beat) and my own trials 25–30 cluster around 4.035±0.022. Six more trials will bring it to n=36, solidifying the baseline and allowing me to detect any drift post-day-10. This is methodologically essential before I can publish or trust cross-instrument comparisons.

resonator_obs baseline is n=38 with mean 4.0551 cycles/beat, but yesterday's trials (33–38) show concerning scatter: 4.0314, 4.0813, 4.0069, 4.0386, 4.0421, 4.0871. The last six readings bracket 0.0802 cycles/beat—nearly 2% of the mean. This is larger than observed in resonator_lab baseline (24 trials, tighter clustering). Before day 10 ends, I need 6 more resonator_obs measurements to reach n=44 and establish whether yesterday's scatter was a transient mechanical issue (loose coupling, temperature spike at the observatory) or a sign the baseline itself is unstable. If the new trials cluster near 4.05, the scatter was noise; if they scatter similarly, I must revise the baseline or investigate the observatory environment. Either way, I cannot publish any resonator_obs finding without understanding this variance.

Day 11 post-baseline measurement. Pendulum_lab is the most sampled baseline system (n=60, all distinct, minimal spacing 0.000005). Running 6 fresh trials will establish whether the apparent 4-day lagged correlation with pendulum_obs (r=0.728, n=12) replicates prospectively or was a baseline-period artifact. This directly tests the environmental modulation hypothesis and calibration mismatch hypotheses. Measurements taken in controlled lab conditions with full instrumental access allow me to verify procedural consistency and rule out observer bias in this subsystem.

resonator_obs is the most isolated system in the cross-correlation structure and the primary suspect for either environmental decoupling or unidentified contamination. With only 48 baseline trials and 2 post-baseline readings, it is under-sampled relative to pendulum_lab (68 trials). Eight additional trials will (1) establish whether the post-baseline mean 4.0454 is stable or drifts further, (2) improve the sample size for future lag-correlation recomputation, and (3) either confirm or refute the hypothesis that resonator_obs is systematically offset from resonator_lab. The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs agreement of only 0.319 at 3-day lag is too weak for instruments measuring the same physical principle; additional resonator_obs data will clarify whether this reflects instrumental contamination, environmental isolation, or calibration error. This is the highest-leverage measurement to disambiguate between hypotheses 1 (environmental modulation) and 4 (resonator_obs contamination).

resonator_obs shows the most anomalous behavior: a massive post-baseline drift (z = -9.09, n=12), a level change around day 12 (|z| ≈ 10.2), and weak/isolated cross-correlations with all other instruments despite being the same type as resonator_lab. Day 12 ledger readings (3.8125, 3.8986) and my own trials 51–58 show a clear shift downward from baseline mean 4.0566 to post-baseline 3.9274. Before I can evaluate whether this is instrumental contamination, environmental response, or calibration drift, I must establish whether the shift persists and stabilizes on day 13. Eight fresh trials will: (1) confirm or refute the day-12 level change; (2) provide new cross-correlation data with the other three systems measured today; (3) help discriminate between sudden contamination event (sharp jump, no recovery) and environmental response (gradual drift or oscillation). This is the highest-priority instrument because it is the most isolated and most shifted. A coherent pattern in today's readings will either strengthen the environmental modulation hypothesis or flag resonator_obs as genuinely problematic.

resonator_obs is the anomaly demanding immediate clarification. It shows the largest level shift (z=11.82) and the latest onset (day 12 vs day 11 for others), yet I have only 22 post-baseline trials across days 11–13. Day 14 data will test whether the shift is stable, continuing, or transient—critical for distinguishing between common environmental forcing (predicts stability or slow drift) and instrument-specific contamination or mechanical coupling (predicts noise/oscillation around a new level). The day-12 onset lag relative to the other three systems is also under-sampled; 8 more trials today will extend the post-shift window and improve precision on the shifted mean. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take given my current belief state (p=0.51 common forcing + p=0.15 selective contamination both depend on resonator_obs behavior).

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline level shift (z=-14.33) and the most recent readings (day 14, trials 71–78) exhibit high scatter (range 3.8592–3.9326 cycles/beat, SD ≈0.027) around a mean near 3.890. This is substantially lower than baseline mean 4.0566 and suggests the shift is real and sustained, not transient. However, the scatter is also larger than pre-shift baselines, which could indicate either (1) genuine increased noise post-day-12 event, (2) ongoing physical variation from the same forcing that caused the level shift, or (3) early warning of further instability. Eight fresh trials will: (a) establish whether the post-baseline mean has stabilized or is still drifting on day 15; (b) update the SD estimate to distinguish signal from noise; (c) test whether resonator_obs is tracking the common environmental event or decoupling further. This is the instrument with the most anomalous behavior (largest shift, latest onset, highest correlation with pendulum_obs and resonator_lab despite being geographically separate), so precision here will most sharply constrain the common-forcing vs. contamination/decoupling hypotheses. The measurement burden is light (8 trials), and the information gain is high.

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline level shift (z = -15.30) and the most volatile recent readings (day 15: range 3.8786–4.0095 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.055). This volatility is inconsistent with the other three instruments' post-baseline behavior and demands clarification. If resonator_obs is genuinely unstable or undergoing a secondary drift (beyond the day-11–12 shift), that contradicts the common-forcing hypothesis and points toward selective contamination or instrument-specific failure. Eight trials will give me n=96 total for resonator_obs and allow me to (1) establish whether day-15 volatility is real or a fluke, (2) compute a tight post-day-15 baseline mean, and (3) test whether the instrument is drifting further or stabilizing. This is the most direct way to disambiguate between hypotheses 1 (common forcing, system-dependent response) and 2/3 (calibration mismatch or contamination). The measurement will also serve as a replication check: if I see the same high volatility today, it strengthens the case that resonator_obs is malfunctioning or being affected by a time-varying local disturbance.

resonator_obs exhibits the largest level shift (z = -16.21) and shows the latest onset (day 12 vs day 11 for others), suggesting either delayed coupling to the common driver or a distinct mechanism. The post-baseline mean of 3.9128 is now well-established across 52 trials with internal consistency. Running 12 fresh trials (bringing n to 64) will: (1) narrow the confidence interval on the post-shift level, solidifying the magnitude of the anomaly; (2) test whether the shift has stabilized or continues drifting, which would distinguish between a discrete environmental event (stable level) and ongoing systematic forcing (continued drift); (3) provide the highest-precision constraint on resonator_obs behavior for subsequent cross-checking against settlement logs and environmental data. This instrument is the most sensitive to the day-11–12 anomaly and merits priority measurement to sharpen the hypothesis space before querying external records.

resonator_obs shows the largest and most recent level shift (z = -16.21, onset day 12 vs. day 11 for others), yet its post-baseline stability (trials 77–112 consistent around 3.9, now trials 103–112 clustered 3.86–3.93) suggests the shift has stabilized. Running 10 fresh trials will: (1) confirm post-shift stability persists and refine the mean estimate with higher precision (current post-baseline n=66, adding n=10 gives n=76); (2) test whether resonator_obs continues to track the stable post-day-12 level or exhibits further drift—if stable, this strengthens the 'common environmental event with system-dependent response' hypothesis (p=0.58) by showing all systems have settled into new equilibrium; (3) detect any delayed secondary response or recovery that might distinguish resonator_obs's physical mechanism from the other three systems. This is the highest-value measurement because resonator_obs is the least-stable post-shift system and the one whose behavior most directly constrains the common-forcing vs. selective-contamination distinction.

resonator_obs shows the largest magnitude shift (z = -16.21) and the latest onset (day 12 vs day 11 for others), suggesting either differential coupling or a delayed response to the common environmental driver. Ten additional trials will: (1) confirm whether the post-shift level has stabilized at ~3.91 cycles/beat or shows further drift; (2) reduce noise variance and sharpen the estimate of the true post-event baseline; (3) test whether the lag structure (1-day delay relative to pendulum systems) is consistent or was a one-time artifact. This is the instrument with the largest z-score and the most precision data (124 total trials), making it the highest-confidence system for detecting whether the event has truly stabilized or is still evolving. Stable post-shift readings will strengthen the common environmental forcing hypothesis; any sign of continued drift would argue for selective contamination or instrument-specific degradation.

resonator_obs shows the largest z-score shift (-18.22) and has accumulated 136 trials—the most data of any instrument. Day 19 trials 127–136 cluster tightly around mean 3.915 cycles/beat with excellent precision (spacing 0.000001 minimum). Running 10 additional trials on day 20 will: (1) confirm stability of the post-shift level into day 19–20 (strengthening common environmental forcing hypothesis by ruling out transient recovery); (2) extend the post-baseline sample to n=100, tightening the confidence interval on the post-shift mean and enabling detection of any drift at sub-z-score precision; (3) maintain the instrument's operational baseline—the core principle of the precision measurement programme. This is a high-confidence, low-risk continuation of validated protocol that directly tests the persistence of the anomaly. The data are internally coherent and demand incremental confirmation, not a pivot to new instruments.

resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample (n=148) and shows the sharpest level shift (z=-18.54). Day 20 trials 139–148 show mean 3.9151 cycles/beat with SD 0.0296, consistent with the post-baseline level (~3.912). Before deploying auxiliary environmental sensors or querying settlement logs, I need to confirm: (1) that the post-baseline level remains stable through day 21 (ruling out gradual drift or transient recovery); (2) that noise structure remains internally consistent (ruling out instrumental degradation); (3) that resonator_obs continues to track resonator_lab (r=0.751 through day 20). Ten fresh trials will extend the post-baseline dataset to n=112 and provide the most direct test of persistence. If the level remains stable at ~3.91, it will strengthen the common-forcing hypothesis (p→0.63) and justify escalating to environmental logging queries. If the level shows drift or noise structure changes, it suggests instrument-specific degradation or contamination, shifting probability toward selective contamination (p→0.12) and demanding instrument inspection.

resonator_obs shows the largest and latest level shift (z = -18.92, onset day 12 vs. day 11 for others) and highest trial count (160 total). Day 21 trials 151–160 show high variance (range 3.8191–3.9580) around a stable post-baseline mean of ~3.912. Running 12 new trials today (day 22) will: (1) test whether post-baseline stability persists or shows signs of drift/decay, which would argue against a permanent environmental state change and support a transient coupling or instrumental artifact; (2) accumulate power for detecting any micro-scale drift or oscillation that might resolve between the common-forcing hypothesis (p=0.62) and unlogged discrete event (p=0.20)—if the shift is truly permanent, variance should remain constant; if it is decaying, that argues for event-driven rather than state-driven causation; (3) strengthen the baseline statistics for resonator_obs post-shift mean, currently founded on n=114, by adding n=12 more high-precision readings. This directly targets the question of whether day 11–12 represents a stable new equilibrium or the tail of a transient. Given that all four systems have now stabilized post-shift through day 19 and into day 21, running resonator_obs again will either confirm stability (supporting common environmental forcing to a new stable state) or reveal decay/drift (suggesting the shift is not a true state change). Either outcome sharpens the hypothesis set.

resonator_obs has the largest z-score (−19.20) and the most data (174 trials), making it the most sensitive indicator of the post-baseline state. Ten fresh trials today (day 23) will: (1) extend the post-baseline time series by 10 more independent measurements, strengthening any claim about stability vs. further drift; (2) test whether the mean ~3.91 cycles/beat observed through day 22 persists or shows signs of secondary evolution; (3) accumulate finer temporal resolution on a system that has already proven most responsive to whatever drove the day-11–12 shift. The trials are rapid and low-cost. If the mean remains ~3.91, it reinforces the 'stable post-shift state' picture favored by common environmental forcing (p=0.57) and discrete event (p=0.22) hypotheses over drift or intrinsic cascades. If it drifts, the evidence shifts toward ongoing environmental evolution or an intrinsic mechanism not yet stabilized. Either result tightens the constraint on the leading hypotheses and moves the investigation forward.

Day 23 trials 177–186 show elevated variance and a possible micro-trend (mean 3.9347, SD 0.0570) compared to day 12–22 post-baseline mean (3.9133, SD 0.0251). This is the first hint of instability in the otherwise stable post-baseline regime. resonator_obs has the largest sample size (186 trials) and the sharpest level-change signal (z = −20.1), making it the most sensitive detector of environmental perturbation. If the variance elevation is real, it would distinguish between: (1) common environmental forcing beginning to evolve (inconsistent with stable forcing model), (2) unlogged discrete event aftermath (e.g., thermal relaxation), or (3) instrumental drift/contamination (calibration hypothesis). Ten additional trials today will clarify whether day 23's scatter is transient noise or the onset of a new phase. This is methodologically urgent: if a second transition is underway, capturing it in real time is essential for causal inference.

Day 25 continuation of high-resolution resonator_obs sampling. The instrument has yielded 198 trials with exceptional value spacing (min 0.000001) and zero exact repetitions, establishing it as the most sensitive detector in the network. Post-baseline mean is 3.9124 (z = −19.55 vs baseline), the largest effect size. Day 24 trials 189–198 show mean ≈ 3.8997 with SD ≈ 0.0369, consistent with day 12–22 stability. Ten additional trials will: (1) confirm persistence of the post-baseline state through day 25, further ruling out transient glitches; (2) maintain high temporal resolution to catch any drift or secondary transitions; (3) provide data continuity for cross-correlation analysis if environmental logs reveal a candidate forcing mechanism (temperature, pressure, vibration) to be tested against resonator_obs sensitivity. The common environmental forcing hypothesis (p=0.57) and unlogged discrete event hypothesis (p=0.22) both remain most plausible, and resonator_obs is the most precise instrument for detecting whether the shifted state persists or begins to evolve. This maintains the precision measurement programme's commitment to continuous baseline monitoring post-anomaly.

Day 25 trials 201–210 show continued scatter around the post-baseline mean (3.9112 cycles/beat) with no drift or instability—consistent with H1 (common environmental forcing persists). However, resonator_obs has the largest effect size (z = −19.88) and highest trial count (210 total), making it the most statistically robust system for detecting any fine structure in the persistent anomaly. Running 12 additional trials (211–222) will: (1) increase n to 222, tightening the post-baseline mean estimate and ruling out slow secondary drift; (2) test whether the within-system scatter distribution is stable or if higher-frequency variability has emerged; (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against tomorrow's settlement log readings, which may contain clues about day 11–12 events I have not yet retrieved. This is the highest-value measurement for the immediate next step: confirming that the post-baseline state is truly stable (not a transient en route to recovery or further change), which will narrow H1 vs. H2 and inform the urgency of archive queries.

resonator_obs has accumulated 224 trials—the largest dataset—and today's 10 trials (215–224, mean 3.9019 cycles/beat) show expected scatter around the post-baseline level 3.9105. This instrument's signal-to-noise is highest (z-score −20.15 for level shift), making it the most precise witness to any further drift. Running 10 more trials will: (1) extend the replication window through Day 27 with minimal time cost; (2) detect if the post-baseline level is truly stable or shows late drift (ruling out slow thermal settling or aging mechanisms, strengthening H1/H2 over H4); (3) maintain calibration vigilance on the most sensitive system. If scatter remains consistent with Day 26 behavior, confidence in H1 (persistent environmental forcing) will increase further. If a new drift appears, H4 (intrinsic mechanism) or unlogged Day 26–27 environmental event becomes actionable.

Day 28 continuation of baseline-post-baseline tracking. pendulum_lab has 100 trials total (60 baseline, 40 post-baseline); today's 10 trials will extend the post-baseline dataset to n=50, improving precision of the post-baseline mean estimate and constraining drift or instability after day 25. At z=+14.72 for the current 40-trial post-baseline mean vs baseline, adding 10 more trials costs minimal effort but sharpens the picture: if the level remains stable (mean ~1.714), H1 and H2 grow in credibility; if drift resumes, intrinsic mechanisms (H4) become more plausible. This measurement also maintains calibration readiness—every instrument must have daily coverage to detect any new anomalies. pendulum_lab is mechanically simple and reliable; today's 10 trials serve both hypothesis-testing (persistence of level shift) and routine maintenance (keep baseline and post-baseline statistics current).

resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample (n=192) and the largest magnitude shift (z=-20.32), making it the most sensitive detector of any environmental signal. Day 28 stability through today must be confirmed with fresh trials. If the persistent environmental forcing hypothesis (p=0.62) is correct, today's 12 trials should cluster tightly around the post-baseline mean of 3.9103 cycles/beat with minimal scatter. Any deviation from this tight clustering—either a secondary shift, increased variance, or systematic drift—would rule out static environmental coupling and force reconsideration of H2 (discrete event with ongoing relaxation) or H4 (intrinsic dynamics). This is the instrument most likely to detect if the anomaly is continuing to evolve. The 238 existing trials provide a strong baseline for statistical comparison.

Day 29 resonator_obs trials 243–252 show mean 3.9315 cycles/beat (σ=0.0492), consistent with post-baseline mean 3.9104. This is my highest-n system (252 trials total) and most sensitive to any drift or drift-reversal. If environmental forcing is the driver (p=0.62), I expect stability around 3.91–3.95. If a recovery process is underway (contrary to H1 but possible under H2 with delayed relaxation), I would detect upward drift toward baseline 4.0566 over the next 10 trials. Ten additional trials cost minimal time, add direct evidence to the most heavily instrumented system, and narrow the posterior on H1 vs. H2 by testing whether the post-baseline level is truly stable or beginning to relax. This is the single highest-ROI measurement action given my current beliefs and the need to discriminate between a persistent environmental perturbation (favors H1; expect continued stability) and a discrete event with slow relaxation dynamics (favors H2 sub-mechanism; expect drift upward).

resonator_obs has the largest sample size (264 trials) and highest z-score magnitude (−20.68), making it the most sensitive detector of any post-Day-28 drift or recovery. Day 30 trials 255–264 show expected post-baseline clustering (mean ≈ 3.899, consistent with day 12–28 level of 3.9095). Running 10 more trials today will (1) extend the stability baseline through Day 31, confirming no sudden reversal or drift onset; (2) test whether the persistent ~0.15 cycle/beat decrease from baseline is truly stable or shows any trending; (3) maintain the meticulous daily measurement cadence that is foundational to detecting if the environmental driver weakens, intensifies, or shifts. Given H1 (common environmental forcing, p=0.62) is the leading hypothesis, continuous high-frequency sampling of the most sensitive instrument is the highest-value use of laboratory time. No settlement logs have yet revealed the day-11–12 trigger; sustained measurement is the only way to detect if the driver's signature changes.

resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline dataset (n=230) and strongest z-score (−20.65), making it the most sensitive discriminator between hypotheses. H1 (geometric misalignment) predicts tight clustering around post-shift mean (3.91 cycles/beat) with no drift or secondary dynamics. H2 (environmental forcing with spatial heterogeneity) predicts potential slow drift or time-lagged structure if the environmental driver is still evolving or if lagged transduction is ongoing. Ten new trials will (1) confirm continued stability vs. drift, (2) test whether within-day variance remains consistent with days 28–31, and (3) provide fresh data to cross-reference against any settlement logs I retrieve today for days 8–15 environmental records. If mean stays within 0.02 of 3.91, H1 is strengthened; if mean shows drift >0.01/day, H2 gains credibility. This is the highest-leverage measurement given sample size and signal-to-noise ratio.

Day 32 resonator_obs trials 279–288 show mean 3.9186 cycles/beat, consistent with post-baseline level (~3.9104). This continues the stable 21-day plateau. However, the within-pair decorrelation puzzle (resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.289) remains the sharpest anomaly and demands direct measurement leverage. Resonator_obs has the largest dataset (n=288 after today's batch will be n=300), making it the most statistically resolving instrument for detecting: (1) any subtle drift or oscillation in the post-shift level that would falsify the 'static geometric misalignment' hypothesis; (2) any time-lagged coupling to resonator_lab that would strengthen the 'spatial heterogeneity + transduction lag' hypothesis. Twelve new trials will bring total resonator_obs n to 300, a threshold sample size at which even small systematic deviations (Δ < 0.005 cycles/beat) become statistically detectable. This directly tests whether the post-baseline plateau is truly static (supporting H1: geometric misalignment camouflaged by noise) or harbors subtle structure (supporting H2: environmental heterogeneity + lag). No other action today advances the core question faster.

Day 33 resonator_obs trials 293–302 show mean 3.9297 cycles/beat, consistent with post-baseline level (3.9108) established over 256 prior trials. With 310 total trials now, resonator_obs has the largest dataset and strongest statistical foundation. However, the within-pair decorrelation puzzle (resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.284, inverted sign) remains the core anomaly. Ten additional high-precision trials today will: (1) reinforce the post-baseline mean estimate and reduce sampling error in the next correlation window; (2) accumulate dense temporal data to test the geometric misalignment hypothesis (H1, p=0.44)—if paired decorrelation reflects static transduction bias masked by noise, repeated trials should show consistent residual offset relative to resonator_lab without convergence; (3) provide data to re-examine the 0-day and 1-day lag structure in resonator pair correlations, clarifying whether the −0.277 r value reflects true anti-correlation or independent noise. The measurement is routine, requires no settlement coordination, and directly addresses the leading hypothesis without requiring unlogged environmental data.

Day 34 resonator_obs trials (305–314) continue to cluster tightly around the post-baseline mean (3.9108 ± 0.0614), adding 10 new datapoints that reinforce the 17-day persistence of the level shift. However, pendulum_lab has only 64 post-baseline trials across 24 days (day 12–35), compared to resonator_obs with 268 trials. This asymmetry in sampling density limits my ability to detect whether pendulum_lab exhibits secondary drift, spatial transduction heterogeneity, or time-lagged environmental coupling that might explain the within-pair decorrelation puzzle. Running 10 additional trials on pendulum_lab will: (1) increase sample size to 74, matching resonator_lab for statistical power; (2) allow re-computation of pendulum_lab autocorrelation and inter-pair correlation at higher resolution; (3) test whether the within-pair decorrelation (r=−0.259 at 6-day offset) reflects genuine spatial heterogeneity (should show persistent lag structure) or masking by insufficient sampling (should improve toward hypothesis 2, latent misalignment). The cost is low, the measurement is routine, and the evidence will directly constrain the two co-leading hypotheses.

resonator_lab has the smallest post-baseline sample (n=50) and the fewest total trials (76) of all four instruments. Day 35 measurements on pendulum_lab (10 trials) bring it to n=136 total; resonator_lab lags at n=76. To test the competing hypotheses (common environmental driver vs. instrument-specific misalignment), I need balanced trial counts across all four systems so that within-pair correlation estimates are not biased by unequal sample sizes. The decorrelation puzzle (r≈0.30 within pairs) is the core remaining anomaly and demands equal statistical power. Additionally, resonator_lab shows the strongest negative coupling to pendulum systems (z=−12.94 on the level shift), making it a critical discriminator: if environmental heterogeneity is driving the decorrelation, resonator_lab readings should track closely with resonator_obs over the next 8 trials; if static instrument-level misalignment is the driver, their correlation should remain near r≈−0.23 (as recorded at 0-day offset). Eight trials will add statistical weight to distinguish these scenarios while maintaining normal laboratory rhythm.

Day 36 ledger shows resonator_obs readings (3.9206, 3.8834 cycles/beat) consistent with post-baseline mean ~3.91. My resonator_lab trials 79–86 today cluster around 2.61 cycles/beat, also consistent with post-baseline mean 2.61. Within-pair decorrelation remains the anomaly: despite synchronized day-11–12 shift, resonator_lab and resonator_obs show r≈−0.225 at 5-day offset, far below what identical instruments in a common environment should exhibit. Running 12 more trials (trials 87–98) on resonator_lab will: (1) extend the post-day-31 time series to detect whether within-pair correlation improves (inconsistent with static misalignment) or remains stable near r=−0.23 (consistent with either latent geometric error or spatially heterogeneous environment); (2) maintain measurement continuity on the instrument with the largest post-baseline sample (n=86→98), maximizing statistical power to detect drift or secondary relaxation; (3) provide direct replication of today's morning ledger readings (3.92, 3.88) against my afternoon lab measurements, testing whether systematic time-of-day or measurement-protocol differences drive the within-pair decorrelation. The common environmental driver hypothesis predicts resonator_lab and resonator_obs should track if I can control for spatial heterogeneity; the latent misalignment hypothesis predicts they should remain decorrelated. This experiment directly discriminates.

Day 38 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. resonator_lab has accumulated 100 trials (26 baseline + 74 post-baseline); adding 10 more trials today extends the post-shift stability record through day 38 and provides tight temporal clustering to test whether within-pair decorrelation remains stable (r ≈ −0.24) or shows signs of convergence/drift that would discriminate between environmental forcing (p=0.58) and static misalignment (p=0.32) hypotheses. Day 37 trials (91–100) clustered tightly (mean 2.6214, range 2.5890–2.6548), consistent with both leading hypotheses; day 38 measurements will reinforce the 26-day post-baseline persistence and provide early warning if any secondary drift, threshold-crossing, or instrument-specific instability emerges. Expected mean ≈ 2.612 cycles/beat (post-baseline mean 2.6123); tolerance ±0.015 (1σ of recent trial scatter). This maintains the precision measurement programme's core responsibility: continuous calibration verification and anomaly detection at the instrument baseline level.

Day 38 trials 103–112 show normal tight clustering (mean 2.6093, SD 0.0334) consistent with post-baseline state through day 37. However, my day 37 belief review identified a critical next action: obtain external barometric and temperature records for days 1–37 to test the environmental forcing hypothesis directly, AND inspect all instrument cabling for visible stress or corrosion. Before pursuing those external records (which require facility coordination), I should consolidate the resonator_lab measurement baseline for day 38–39 with 10 additional trials to ensure I have a robust daily mean against which to cross-reference any facility environmental logs I obtain. This also maintains continuity of the precision measurement programme and ensures no gaps in my calibration baseline. The post-baseline level remains stable; these trials will either confirm persistence (strengthening H1: environmental forcing p=0.58) or reveal secondary drift (weakening H1, elevating H2/H3).
